items.title: Birth at Mhow, 14 April 1891
items.location: Mhow (now Dr. Ambedkar Nagar), Madhya Pradesh
items.source: Standard published biographies; Dr. Ambedkar Janmabhoomi memorial records
items.description: Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was born on 14 April 1891 at Mhow in the Central Provinces, into a Mahar family. His father, Ramji Maloji Sakpal, served in the British Indian Army. His birthplace at Mhow is today a national memorial.

media.label: Artistic visualization — not a historical photograph

items.title: School Years and Early Discrimination
items.author: B. R. Ambedkar (autobiographical accounts)
items.source: B. R. Ambedkar, autobiographical fragment commonly titled 'Waiting for a Visa'
items.description: At school, young Bhimrao suffered caste discrimination — segregated seating, and dependence on others even for drinking water. He later recorded these experiences in autobiographical writings that are widely used to teach the human cost of untouchability. In 1907 he passed his matriculation from Elphinstone High School, Bombay.

items.title: B.A., Bombay University, 1912
items.source: University of Bombay records as cited in standard biographies
items.description: Ambedkar graduated from Elphinstone College, University of Bombay, in 1912 with a degree in economics and political science — among the earliest members of his community to reach university education.

items.title: Columbia University, New York (1913–1916)
items.source: Columbia University records; standard biographies
items.description: With a scholarship from the Maharaja of Baroda, Sayajirao Gaekwad III, Ambedkar studied at Columbia University, earning his M.A. in 1915 and later a Ph.D. (1927). He described his time at Columbia as a period of intellectual freedom and equality he had never before experienced.

items.title: London School of Economics & Gray's Inn
items.source: LSE and Gray's Inn records; standard biographies
items.description: Ambedkar enrolled at the London School of Economics and at Gray's Inn to study law. He was called to the Bar by Gray's Inn in 1922 and was awarded a D.Sc. (Economics) by the University of London in 1923. His London years made him one of the most highly qualified scholars of his generation.

items.title: Professor at Sydenham College, 1918
items.source: Standard published biographies
items.description: Ambedkar served as Professor of Political Economy at Sydenham College of Commerce and Economics, Bombay. Students valued his teaching, though caste prejudice among colleagues persisted.

items.title: Mooknayak — 'Leader of the Voiceless', 1920
items.author: B. R. Ambedkar (editor)
items.source: Historical press records; standard biographies
items.description: Ambedkar founded the Marathi fortnightly Mooknayak ('Leader of the Voiceless') in January 1920 to articulate the grievances of the oppressed and to campaign for social equality. Journalism remained one of his primary instruments of public education.

items.title: Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha, 1924
items.source: Standard published biographies
items.description: Ambedkar founded the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (Depressed Classes Welfare Association) to promote education and socio-economic improvement among the depressed classes, opening hostels, libraries and study circles.

items.title: Mahad Satyagraha, 1927
items.source: Contemporary press reports; standard biographies
items.description: In March 1927 Ambedkar led a peaceful satyagraha at the Chavdar Tank in Mahad, asserting the right of the so-called untouchables to draw public water. In December 1927, at a second conference at Mahad, the Manusmriti was ceremonially burned as a symbolic rejection of caste authority.

items.title: Kalaram Temple Satyagraha, Nashik, 1930
items.source: Standard published biographies
items.description: The Kalaram Temple satyagraha (1930–1935) sought entry for Dalits into the Kalaram temple at Nashik. The campaign, conducted non-violently, became a landmark assertion of equal civic dignity, even as Ambedkar's thinking evolved beyond temple entry as the central goal.

items.title: Round Table Conferences, London, 1930–32
items.source: Proceedings of the Round Table Conferences (public records)
items.description: Ambedkar represented the depressed classes at the three Round Table Conferences in London, forcefully arguing for constitutional safeguards and separate electorates. His interventions established him as the foremost political voice of the depressed classes.

items.title: Poona Pact, 24 September 1932
items.source: Text of the Poona Pact (public historical record)
items.description: After the British Communal Award granted separate electorates to the depressed classes, Mahatma Gandhi fasted in Yerwada Jail in protest. The resulting Poona Pact (1932) between Ambedkar and caste-Hindu leaders replaced separate electorates with reserved seats for the depressed classes within joint electorates — the ancestor of today's legislative reservation system.

items.title: Independent Labour Party, 1936
items.source: Electoral and party records; standard biographies
items.description: Ambedkar founded the Independent Labour Party in 1936. In the 1937 provincial elections the party won 15 seats in the Bombay Legislative Assembly, campaigning on workers' rights, abolition of exploitative systems, and social justice.

items.title: Labour Member, Viceroy's Executive Council, 1942–46
items.source: Government of India records; standard biographies
items.description: As Member for Labour, Ambedkar advanced landmark labour reforms — including the eight-hour working day and social security measures — and initiated institutions for technical education and employment exchanges.

items.title: First Law Minister of Independent India, 1947
items.source: Government of India records
items.description: On 15 August 1947 Ambedkar became Independent India's first Minister of Law and Justice in Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru's cabinet, and on 29 August 1947 he was elected Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly.

items.title: Chairman of the Drafting Committee
items.source: Constituent Assembly Debates (official record)
items.description: As Chairman of the seven-member Drafting Committee, Ambedkar steered the preparation of the Constitution through nearly three years of debate, scholarship and compromise. In his closing address on 26 November 1949, Constituent Assembly president Dr. Rajendra Prasad said the Assembly could not have made a better choice than to place Ambedkar on the Drafting Committee and make him its Chairman.

items.title: The Preamble of the Constitution of India
items.author: The Constituent Assembly of India
items.source: Constitution of India (public domain text)
items.description: WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens: JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation; IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION. (Text as currently in force. The words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'integrity' were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976; the Preamble adopted on 26 November 1949 read 'Sovereign Democratic Republic' and 'unity of the Nation'.)

media.label: Document facsimile — digitization placeholder; text is the Preamble as currently in force

items.title: Fundamental Rights (Part III of the Constitution)
items.author: The Constituent Assembly of India
items.source: Constitution of India, Articles 12–35
items.description: The Fundamental Rights guarantee equality before law (Art. 14), prohibit discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth (Art. 15), abolish untouchability (Art. 17), protect freedoms of speech and expression (Art. 19), and life and personal liberty (Art. 21). Ambedkar called Article 32 — the right to constitutional remedies — 'the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it' (Constituent Assembly Debates).

items.title: Adoption of the Constitution: 26 Nov 1949 / 26 Jan 1950
items.source: Constituent Assembly records; official commemoration records
items.description: The Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949 (now observed as Constitution Day / Samvidhan Divas), and it came into force on 26 January 1950 (Republic Day), making India a sovereign democratic republic with the world's lengthiest written national constitution of the time.

items.title: Representation & Safeguards: Legacy of the Poona Pact
items.source: Poona Pact (1932); Constitution of India (Part XVI)
items.description: The Poona Pact's reserved seats evolved into constitutional provisions for the representation of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in legislatures, alongside public-service safeguards — one of the longest-running systems of affirmative representation in the democratic world.

items.title: The Problem of the Rupee (1923)
items.author: B. R. Ambedkar
items.source: P. S. King & Son, London (published edition); LSE thesis records
items.description: Ambedkar's D.Sc. dissertation, 'The Problem of the Rupee: Its Origin and Its Solution', analyzed Indian currency and exchange and is cited among the scholarly works anticipating the case for a central bank in India.

items.title: Annihilation of Caste (1936)
items.author: B. R. Ambedkar
items.source: Self-published edition, 1936; subsequent critical editions
items.description: Written as a presidential address for the Jat-Pat Todak Mandal of Lahore — an invitation withdrawn after the organizers read the text — 'Annihilation of Caste' is among the most influential critiques of the caste system ever published, and remains a foundational text in the study of social justice.

items.title: Who Were the Shudras? (1946)
items.author: B. R. Ambedkar
items.source: Thacker & Co., 1946
items.description: A historical inquiry into the origins of the Shudra varna, arguing from textual sources that the Shudras were originally a ruling people degraded by conflict with the Brahmins — an example of Ambedkar's methodological commitment to evidence-based history.

items.title: The Buddha and His Dhamma (published 1957)
items.author: B. R. Ambedkar
items.source: Published posthumously by the People's Education Society, 1957
items.description: Ambedkar's final major work, a modern retelling of the life and teaching of the Buddha, was published posthumously in 1957 and serves as a sacred text for Navayana Buddhists.

items.title: Embracing Buddhism — Deekshabhoomi, 14 Oct 1956
items.source: Contemporary reports; Deekshabhoomi memorial records
items.description: On Ashoka Vijaya Dashami, 14 October 1956, Ambedkar formally embraced Buddhism at a ceremony in Nagpur together with several hundred thousand followers, initiating the Navayana ('new vehicle') Buddhist movement. The site is today Deekshabhoomi, one of the most visited monuments in Asia.

items.title: Mahaparinirvan — 6 December 1956
items.source: Contemporary reports; standard biographies
items.description: Dr. Ambedkar passed away in his sleep on 6 December 1956 at his home on Alipur Road, Delhi. The day is observed by millions as Mahaparinirvan Diwas. He was posthumously awarded the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honour, in 1990.

items.title: Dr. Ambedkar Janmabhoomi Memorial, Mhow
items.author: Government of Madhya Pradesh
items.source: Memorial authority records; press reports of the 2008 inauguration
items.description: The birthplace memorial at Mhow enshrines the house and site where Dr. Ambedkar was born in 1891. In-game: stylized digital reconstruction.

items.title: Chaitya Bhoomi, Mumbai
items.source: Chaitya Bhoomi Trust records; press records
items.description: Chaitya Bhoomi at Dadar, Mumbai, beside the sea, marks the site of Dr. Ambedkar's final rites. Every 6 December it draws one of the largest peaceful public gatherings in the world. In-game: stylized digital reconstruction.

items.title: Deekshabhoomi, Nagpur
items.author: Architect Sheo Dan Mal
items.source: Deekshabhoomi memorial records; architectural press records
items.description: Deekshabhoomi marks the ground of the 1956 mass conversion. Its great two-storey hemispherical stupa — among the largest hollow stupas in the world — was designed by architect Sheo Dan Mal. In-game: stylized digital reconstruction.

items.title: Dr. Ambedkar National Memorial, 26 Alipur Road, Delhi
items.author: Government of India
items.source: Prime Minister's Office release, 13 April 2018
items.description: The house at 26 Alipur Road, where Dr. Ambedkar spent his final years, is preserved as the Dr. Ambedkar National Memorial (Mahaparinirvan Bhoomi), inaugurated by the Prime Minister on 13 April 2018. In-game: stylized digital reconstruction.

items.title: Dr. Ambedkar Park, Lucknow
items.author: Government of Uttar Pradesh
items.source: Government of Uttar Pradesh records
items.description: A monumental memorial complex in red sandstone honouring Dr. Ambedkar and other social reformers, with elephants, domes and a central memorial — among the largest memorial landscapes in India. In-game: stylized digital reconstruction.

items.title: Ambedkar House, Primrose Hill, London
items.author: Government of Maharashtra
items.source: Government of Maharashtra acquisition records, 2015
items.description: The London house where Ambedkar lived while studying (1921–22) was acquired by the Government of Maharashtra in 2015 and opened as a memorial and museum. In-game: stylized digital reconstruction.

items.title: “Educate, Agitate, Organise”
items.author: Attributed to B. R. Ambedkar
items.source: Widely attributed slogan of the movement (attribution noted)
items.description: The triad 'Educate, Agitate, Organise' is the most famous motto associated with Dr. Ambedkar's movement — a compact program for social change through learning, advocacy and collective organization. (Presented as an attributed slogan, not a sourced quotation.)

items.title: Context: 'The very soul of the Constitution'
items.author: B. R. Ambedkar
items.source: Constituent Assembly Debates, Vol. VII (official record)
items.description: Speaking in the Constituent Assembly on 9 December 1948 on Article 32 (draft Article 25) (the right to move the Supreme Court to enforce fundamental rights), Ambedkar said he was glad the House had realized the importance of the article, which he called 'the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it'.

items.title: Global Commemoration & the Statue of Social Justice
items.source: Government of Andhra Pradesh inauguration records (January 2024); United Nations commemoration records (New York, April 2016)
items.description: Dr. Ambedkar is commemorated across India and internationally — his birth anniversary (14 April, Ambedkar Jayanti) was commemorated at the United Nations in New York in 2016, and large memorial statues have been raised in recent years, including the 125-ft 'Statue of Social Justice' at Vijayawada, inaugurated in January 2024. A memorial to him at Mumbai's Indu Mills has been announced and is under development. This entry records the reach of his legacy.
